accuracy.reason: Claims expose stale hits, independent copies, and concurrent refill limits, and agree with the checked primary sources. Both packet diagrams accurately depict their operations.

evidence.quote: A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.

mechanisms.reason: Actors, cache state, and cause/effect are explicit for read paths, writes, eviction and overload. Sharing one in-progress lookup explains how duplicate source work is reduced.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: The product scenario progresses from repeated work and source ownership through reads, keys, changing data, placement, failure, and a workload decision. Concepts are introduced before their consequences.

evidence.quote: A popular product page keeps asking the API for the same name, description, and price. Each request repeats a database lookup.

decisions.reason: Benefits, costs, acceptable staleness, network placement, bounded fallback, and the reason to decline a cache are explained in usable terms.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: New terms are tied to concrete operations in plain language. TTL is distinguished from refreshing; non-atomic operations are immediately explained through the overlap that matters.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

outcomes.reason: C1: repeated guides avoid an 80 ms build via 2 ms hits, using slide 1. C2: key includes station and language, applying slide 3. C3-C4: traces application hit return and miss database read, copy storage, and return using slide 2. C5: explicitly assigns cache-aside to the application and enumerates checking/filling plus database work on misses; this operation trace identifies the additional work without requiring a preferred cost phrase.

C1-C2: traces old hours being stored after deletion, supported by slides 2/4 and the supplied order. C3: rejects the freshness guarantee using slide 4. C4: bypasses the copy and reads authoritative data, transferring slide 4 validation to this endpoint with the declared database-commit prerequisite.

C1: stale hit at 12:03, source fetch at 12:11. C2: source fetch at 12:05 after eviction. C3: denies guaranteed residency, freshness and automatic refresh. C4: differentiates time expiration from freeing memory and places loading at the next request, not the removal event. Slides 2/5 support every step.

C1: other local copies remain old. C2: a single shared entry fits one deletion under the explicit assumptions. C3: contrasts local process copies with a network lookup. C4: identifies network and operating costs and denies automatic freshness. Slide 6 supports the comparison and slide 2 the refill.

C1-C2: explains duplicate simultaneous source reads and one shared in-progress lookup (slide 7). C3: compares 10,000 potential reads with 500 capacity. C4: caps aggregate fallback at 500 and rejects excess, explaining eliminated work. C5: this complete response does not rely on stale data, so no stale-copy mechanism is required. The optional accessible-copy suggestion alone does not establish where the copy survives and receives no additional credit.

C1-C2: declines because no second read can benefit. C3: uses 2 ms and ten reads/second against the given budgets. C4: identifies an extra store and managed copy. C5: conditions reconsideration on repeated reads and assessed latency/load benefit rather than repetition alone. Slides 1/8 support this reasoning.

sourceChecks.claim: Reusable copies reduce repeated source work and latency; the guidance supports this while preserving source ownership.
The source algorithm supports application check, miss fetch, fill and return; the packet read-path diagram agrees.
The source explains application cache-aside and distinct structured keys; separating answer-changing inputs follows this model.
The source disclaims cache/source consistency. Separate fetch/fill operations permit the stated overlap; authoritative validation avoids trusting stale copies.
Redis supports memory-triggered eviction, LRU, noeviction errors and evicting TTL-bearing entries, so TTL cannot guarantee residency.
Expiration does not refresh source data: Redis separates expiration from eviction; the linked Azure/AWS pages describe timed retention, not automatic reloading.
AWS supports separate local copies, shared external entries, network/operating costs and residual consistency limits.
AWS explains coalescing, outage load surges, capped fallback with rejection, and testing without caching.
The guidance supports measuring benefits, favoring repeated costly reads, and treating low reuse as a poor candidate.
